'''Akachari''', or '''Cari''' (occasionally 'Kari', 'Chariar' or 'Sare'), is an extinct dialect of the [[Northern Andamanese language]] that was spoken by the [[Cari people]], one of the dozen [[Great Andamanese people]]s.<ref name="ethin">{{Cite web |url=http://www.christusrex.org/www3/ethno/Inda.html |title=Ethnologue India |access-date=12 July 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100715202610/http://www.christusrex.org/www3/ethno/Inda.html |archive-date=15 July 2010 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name="weber7">George Weber (~2009), ''[http://www.andaman.org/BOOK/chapter7/text7.htm Numbers] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120531230544/http://www.andaman.org/BOOK/chapter7/text7.htm |date=31 May 2012 }}''. Chapter 7 of [http://www.andaman.org/BOOK/text-group-BodyChapters.htm The Andamanese] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120805204050/http://www.andaman.org/BOOK/app-a/a-portman.htm |date=5 August 2012 }}. Accessed on 12 July 2012.</ref><ref name="Abbi2009">{{cite journal|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/222414027|title=Is Great Andamanese genealogically and typologically distinct from Onge and Jarawa?|last=Abbi|first=Anvita|journal=Language Sciences|volume=31|issue=6|pages=791–812|year=2009|doi=10.1016/j.langsci.2008.02.002}}</ref>

In the 19th century, the Cari lived on the north coast of [[North Andaman]], as well as on [[Landfall Island]] and other nearby small islands. By 1994, the population had been reduced to two women aged over 50, living with the other few surviving Great Andamanese on [[Strait Island]]. Aka-Cari became extinct with the death of Licho in April 2020.<ref>{{cite news|title=The Pandemic Also Threatens Endangered Languages|url=https://blogs.scientificamerican.com/voices/the-pandemic-also-threatens-endangered-languages/|website=scientificamerican.com|publisher=Scientific American|last=Abbi|first=Anvita|date=30 April 2020|access-date=24 January 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Remembering Licho, the Last Speaker of the Sare Language|url=https://terralingua.org/2020/04/30/remembering-licho-the-last-speaker-of-sare-a-great-andamanese-language/|website=terralingua.org|date=30 April 2020|access-date=24 January 2023}}</ref><ref name="gob">A. N. Sharma (2003), ''[https://books.google.com/books?id=WEztW7c0CqQC&pg=PA62 Tribal Development in the Andaman Islands]'', page 62. Sarup & Sons, New Delhi.</ref>

==History==
The Cari population at the time of first European contacts (in the 1790s) has been estimated at 100 individuals, out of perhaps 3500 Great Andamanese.<ref name="weber7"/>
Like other [[Andamanese people]]s, the Cari were decimated during colonial and post-colonial times, by diseases, [[alcohol (drug)|alcohol]], colonial warfare and loss of territory. The population was down to 39 individuals in the 1901 census, falling to 36 in 1911, 17 in 1921, and 9 in 1931.<ref name="gob"/>

In 1949 any remaining Cari were relocated, together with all other surviving Great Andamanese, to a reservation on [[Bluff Island (Andaman)|Bluff island]]; and then again in 1969 to a reservation on [[Strait Island]].<ref name="mann">Rann Singh Mann (2005), [https://books.google.com/books?id=FPX6wiuZ3ikC&pg=PA149 Andaman and Nicobar Tribes Restudied: Encounters and Concerns], page 149. Mittal Publications. {{ISBN|81-8324-010-0}}</ref>

By 1994, the tribe was reduced to only two women, aged 57 and 59, and therefore was on its way to extinction.<ref name="gob"/> The last speaker, a woman called Licho, died from chronic tuberculosis on 4 April 2020 in Shadipur, [[Port Blair]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=International|first=Survival|date=1 June 2020|title=The last speaker of the Sare language has died|url=https://medium.com/@survivalinternational/the-last-speaker-of-the-sare-language-has-died-767013159e83|access-date=28 June 2020|website=Medium|language=en}}</ref>

They are a designated [[Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes|Scheduled Tribe]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://censusindia.gov.in/Tables_Published/SCST/ST%20Lists.pdf |page=27 |title=List of notified Scheduled Tribes |publisher=Census India |access-date=15 December 2013 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131107225208/http://censusindia.gov.in/Tables_Published/SCST/ST%20Lists.pdf |archive-date=7 November 2013 }}</ref>

==Grammar==
The Great Andamanese languages are [[agglutinative]] languages, with an extensive prefix and suffix system.<ref name=Templ>Temple, Richard C. (1902). ''A Grammar of the Andamanese Languages, being Chapter IV of Part I of the Census Report on the Andaman and Nicobar Islands''. Superintendent's Printing Press: Port Blair.</ref> They have a distinctive [[noun class]] system based largely on body parts, in which every [[noun]] and [[adjective]] may take a [[Prefix (linguistics)|prefix]] according to which body part it is associated with (on the basis of shape, or functional association). Thus, for instance, the *aka- at the beginning of the language names is a prefix for objects related to the [[tongue]].<ref name="Templ"/> 

Body parts are [[Inalienable possession|inalienably possessed]], requiring a [[possessive adjective]] [[Prefix (linguistics)|prefix]] to complete them, so one cannot say "head" alone, but only "my, or his, or your, etc. head".

'This' and 'that' are distinguished as ''k-'' and ''t-''.

Judging from the available sources, the Andamanese languages have only two [[cardinal number (linguistics)|cardinal number]]s — [[1 (number)|one]] and [[2 (number)|two]] — and their entire numerical lexicon is one, two, one more, some more, and all.<ref name="Templ"/>
